Name: Migrating / Кочёвка
Description: In this brief excerpt Ija Krivoshapkina tells about her earliest memories of life in a reindeer herd,1 namely how she migrated with her parents as a three-year old. In summer or early autumn she sat on her riding reindeer (uːʨak; Figure 1.1; see Figure 3.22 in Section 3.3 for a photo of an infant’s saddle ɵːɲeː) in a caravan led by her father, and in late autumn and winter she and her younger brother sat in a covered sled (kibitka; Figure 1.2) driven by her mother. At this time their dog flushed out a snow sheep (Ovis nivicola, also known as Siberian bighorn sheep) which her father was able to bag.
Citation: Ija Krivoshapkina. 2026. Migrating / Кочёвка. In Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Migrating with an infant / Кочёвка с младенцем
Description: In this excerpt, Ekaterina Krivoshapkina tells how she took her one-year-old son to the reindeer herd, where he spent his early years. She explains how the Evens migrate by reindeer caravan in summer (Figure 2.1), with a special rein- deer, the bebeːruk, carrying the baby’s cradle (a cradle is shown in Figure 3.23 in Section 3.3), whereas in winter the infant is transported by kibitka (the covered sled illustrated in Figure 1.2 above). This text contains several evaluatives derived from descriptive verbs, amongst others the only spontaneously produced form of the ‘tenderness’ marker - ɟaːgagaj (in line 36).
Citation: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina. Migrating with an infant / Кочёвка с младенцем. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Childhood in the herd / Детство в стаде
Description: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina remembers her childhood in the reindeer herd. Every year her mother, who worked as a teacher in the Sebjan-Küöl school, would take her and her brother to spend the summer with their father who was a brigade leader. They would go together with a big group of cousins, and the children joined in the reindeer herding: the older children would join the night shifts (iaβʨi- ‘herd at night’), and the younger children would help with the daytime herding (kɵsʨi- ‘herd by day’). In this way they learned how to find suitable pasture for the reindeer, how to treat them if they fell ill, and how to milk reindeer cows. In the text “Reindeer milk products” (Text 5) she explains what they do with the reindeer milk.
Citation: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina. Childhood in the herd / Детство в стаде. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Dogs / Собаки
Description: In this very short fragment Ekaterina Krivoshapkina explains about the different dogs they have: dogs that help with herding and dogs that help with hunting. Note that it is rather unusual for Evens to have herding dogs (Alekseeva 2020: 47), a phenomenon that is generally considered characteristic of reindeer herding peoples west of the Yenisey (Tan-Bogoraz 1932: 37, Vasilevič & Levin 1951: 75).
Citation: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina. Dogs / Собаки. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Reindeer milk products / Блюда из оленьего молока
Description: In the original recording, this excerpt is the continuation of Ekaterina Krivoshap- kina’s childhood memories: after explaining how she learned to milk reindeer (Text 3, lines 35-42), she here goes on to say that she nowadays milks many rein- deer every day in summer. She then explains about the different products they make from reindeer milk. Whipped milk is called kɵrʨek – after adding berries it is similar to yoghurt. The milk is also gradually heated and eaten warm, or spread on bread after having cooled off. Another product that is occasionally made is keːbel, a kind of cheese; for this, rennet is needed that is taken from a snow sheep lamb’s stomach. Reindeer milk has a much higher fat content than cow’s milk, with 11-15% at mid-lactation and reaching 20% in late lactation, with 12-13% protein content. Furthermore, the fat globules form a more stable emulsion, explaining why it gets thick enough to spread when boiled. The change in chemical composition over the lactation period has an influence on the use made of the milk: “Normally the milk from the first part of lactation was consumed fresh; the second part was mainly used for cheese production...” (Holand et al. 2006: 358).
Citation: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina. Reindeer milk products / Блюда из оленьего молока. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Taming reindeer / Обучение оленей
Description: In this fragment Ekaterina Krivoshapkina explains how her father and her brother tame the working reindeer so that they come when they are called. Reindeer are relatively easy to tame early in their life, becoming increasingly stubborn as the months go by (Holand et al. 2006: 358). So when the calves are just a few months old (called eːnken) they are tied to trees and given some salt. In this way, they are used to receiving salt, which they crave, from their handlers. The cows, too, are trained to accept being tied up so that they can be milked. Calves of tame cows are tamer than the calves of the delmiʨe, the semi-domesticated bulk of the herd. Taming reindeer to such a degree takes a lot of time and dedication,1 which explains Ekaterina Krivoshapkina’s pride in her family’s achievement.
Citation: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina. Taming reindeer / Обучение оленей. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Hide preparation / Обработка шкур
Description: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina explains how they prepare animal hide in the herd, by scraping it with a koːʨaj (see Figure 3.26 in Section 3.3), soaking it with hilte (rotten larch, Figure 7.1), and softening it (moŋŋa-) with a kerde (see Figure 3.26 in Section 3.3). However, in town she lacks the hilte and has to use brewed tea instead. She also doesn’t have a kerde, but is hoping that her mother will send her one from the village. She will then be able to prepare the hide from reindeer legs (ohol), so that she can have fur boots (unta) sewn from them. Such fur boots are an absolute necessity in the extremely cold Yakutian winters (Figure 7.2).
Citation: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina. Hide preparation / Обработка шкур. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Eating velvet antlers / Панты
Description: In this extract Ekaterina Krivoshapkina explains about some of the food products traditionally eaten by Evens. A delicacy is roasted velvet antlers (nimeːt). The young antlers of reindeer are soft and are sawed off and eaten after burning off the velvet in the fire. Even later the endpoints of the antlers are soft and can be eaten, although the larger part of the antler body grows hard and bony. The velvet antlers are cut in dry sunny weather and chewed and sucked with relish by children. The beneficial properties of velvet antlers are known to Russian (and Southern Korean, Turaev 2017: 197) companies who produce tonics from them. Another source of vitamins in the past was the root of the Siberian lily (nubaː) which was dug up and eaten raw or cooked.
Citation: Ekaterina Krivoshapkina. Eating velvet antlers / Панты. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Unexpected visits / Неожиданные гости
Description: For details about the recording and the speaker please see the introduction to Text 1. The complete recording with full transcription, translation, and glossing can be accessed at: https://hdl.handle.net/1839/7a0cc8f1- 03e4- 4f95- b129- 2937691791e4.
Citation: Ija Krivoshapkina. Unexpected visits / Неожиданные гости. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Bear / Медведь
Description: This story captures very vividly what could happen on the long trek from the herd to the village when the children had to go to school. A bear came upon the overnight camp where the narrator, who was then ten years old, and her seven- year-old sister were on their own, while their father had gone to try and shoot a snow sheep. He came running and luckily managed to scare the bear away by setting fire to reindeer moss, but not before a very dramatic confrontation between the father and the bear across the campfire. This narrative contains numerous examples of different augmentatives, no- tably the only examples in the Lamunkhin Even corpus of the finite Verbal Aug- mentative -baha as well as several instances of the Augmentative converb -jaːɟi  (see lines 52 and 69 for examples of both forms). It also contains several exam- ples of the Assertive mood borrowed from Sakha (Yakut) - see lines (47), (50), and (66).
Citation: Marta Krivoshapkina. Bear / Медведь. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Snow sheep migration / Уямканы
Description: This tells of another encounter with wildlife on the way back from the reindeer herd for the start of the schoolyear. In this case, Ija Krivoshapkina was travelling to the village with her father and younger brother in the company of a fellow reindeer herder who was taking his grandchildren to school. Their path was crossed by a herd of snow sheep (also known as Siberian bighorn sheep, Ovis nivicola) such as she’d never seen before or since. They spent an extra night along the way to shoot several of them, bagging so much meat that they had to bury some of it along the way, going back to fetch it later. During the translation sessions Ija Krivoshapkina elaborated on a few points; these explanations are added to footnotes (1, 3, 6, 8, 9).
Citation: Ija Krivoshapkina. Snow sheep migration / Уямканы. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Stuck in the herd / Застряли в стаде
Description: This narrative tells of the end of a summer that Raisa Alekseeva spent in the reindeer herd with her children and husband and of their troubles with returning to the village. After first waiting for a helicopter, they were told that this had been cancelled and that they should make their way towards the village by themselves – only to hear while they were on the way that the helicopter had come to the herd after all, but that they had missed it. The experience was made more arduous by the fact that a bear had eaten most of their food stores; in addition, the weather turned cold and it started to snow, but they only had light tents to sleep in. It was only after returning to the herd and waiting for several days that they were finally picked up and flown to the village, where the school year had already started. The anecdote thus sheds light on the way that traditional elements of the nomadic lifestyle (migrating by reindeer and horse, sleeping in tents, cooking over a fire) combine with modernity introduced during Soviet times, namely the helicopter that flies families from outlying reindeer herding territories to the village. The text contains several examples of the Necessitive borrowed from Sakha (Yakut); see lines (4), (6), and (18).
Citation: Raisa Alekseeva. Stuck in the herd / Застряли в стаде. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Aufeis / Наледь
Description: text provides a very vivid account of what can be involved when travel- ling in the traditional way by reindeer sled. Zoja Stepanova tells about a trip in winter from the village to the reindeer herd to visit her father. She was travelling with her younger brother and her sister-in-law when suddenly her brother’s sled broke through aufeis (a thin layer of ice that forms when water flows over frozen rivers), landing her brother in water. Fortunately they had only just passed a tent along the way that was set up for travellers and were able to make their way back there, where they were able to dry their wet clothes at the fire. The rivers leading to Sebjan-Küöl are notorious for their stretches of aufeis, making them hazardous to travel on (Figures 13.1 and 13.2). Truckers who make the journey tend to travel in groups, so that they can pull each other’s trucks out of the icy water when they break through the thin sheet of top ice.
Citation: Zoja Stepanova. Aufeis / Наледь. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Hunting tradition / Как стать хорошим охотником
Description: This short text contains a little anecdote about how the speaker’s younger brother had twice as a child tried to observe the custom of sharing his first hunting spoils with a respected older visitor. Unfortunately, this visitor got star- tled at the touch of the dead animals (first a bird and later a tarbagan marmot) and dropped them both times – much to the dismay of the little boy, who was worried that her behaviour would jinx him (majukan-). The text also contains interesting information about the traditional Even system of avoiding respected people’s names and teknonymy.
Citation: Zoja Stepanova. Hunting tradition / Как стать хорошим охотником. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Good fortune / Счастливая прогулка
Description: In this excerpt, Ija Krivoshapkina tells how she and her family went out for a walk in a place called Kuːnikit (see Text 9 for another episode that took place there) during her father’s day off and unexpectedly came upon two snow sheep. Her father was able to shoot both of them, providing the children with such rare delicacies as the eyes and the raw fat from the back of the head. They took the intestines and liver back with them to camp that day and feasted upon their return, and went back later to fetch the meat. This episode took place in the early 1990s, after the collapse of the Soviet Union, when products and especially meat were scarce. Obtaining so much good meat at once was indeed a stroke of extremely good luck.
Citation: Ija Krivoshapkina. Good fortune / Счастливая прогулка. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: A life with reindeer / Жить с оленями
Description: Evdokija Adukanova tells how she left to get married when she was 16 or 17 years old. She first had to travel by dog sled from her parents’ home in Laučan to the village called Tvajan (Figure 1), where she waited for the reindeer herd that she and her future husband were going to join to come by on their migration route. She then spent many years in a reindeer herd, working first as a reindeer herder and later as a yurt worker, always travelling by reindeer. When she wasn’t looking after the reindeer or cooking pots of food for the herders, she would prepare hides and sew traditional Even leather and fur clothes.
Citation: Evdokija Adukanova. A life with reindeer / Жить с оленями. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Childhood in a reindeer herd / Детство в табуне
Description: Pelageja Banakanova tells about her childhood and adolescence, which she spent in a reindeer herd together with her parents. Since there were too few herders for the number of reindeer, she started to work from age 12. She helped her father herd by day, learning everything about reindeer, but she also helped her mother prepare hides and sew. Even though they didn’t have much to eat, and even though they migrated all the time, she considers that life in the herd was very good, and would like to go back if only she were younger.
Citation: Pelageja Banakanova. Childhood in a reindeer herd / Детство в табуне. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Herding reindeer / Работа оленевода
Description: Gennadij Solodikov provides a reindeer herder’s perspective on reindeer herding in Kamchatka. They get up very early and accompany the herd on foot, drinking tea while there. If all is quiet they might even try to shoot some ducks. The herd is driven back to the camp at lunchtime, where the reindeer circle continuously (Figure 3.1), while the herders eat lunch and drink tea, before taking the herd back out to graze (Figure 3.2). Lame and ill reindeer are taken out of the herd and treated at the camp, while less severely affected animals are treated in the herd.
Citation: Gennadij Solodikov. Herding reindeer / Работа оленевода. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: In the reindeer herd / Работа чумработницы
Description: With this text Valentina Axmetova provides a yurt worker’s perspective of life in a Kamchatkan reindeer herd. In the winter the herd can be in a large pasture for several months at a time, and so the herders can construct a large and comfortable yurt. In this yurt the yurt worker cooks meat and various dishes introduced by Russians like borsht, plov (an Uzbek-style rice dish), or pelmeni (a type of ravioli). She also bakes bread on the stove (Figure 4.1) – and since she uses her bumpy pots as baking pans the bread comes out very pretty, with patterns from the bumps. In summer they have to move every few days, because the grass gets trampled by the reindeer hooves. Everything is packed the evening before, and Valentina Axmetova cooks a pot of meat (Figure 4.2 and 4.3). After breakfast the last dishes are packed, the yurt is taken down, the horses are saddled, and they move on (Figure 4.4). Upon arriving at the new camp the fire is lit and the yurt is put up again (Figure 4.5). They migrate as early as possible to avoid the heat of day, when horse flies and mosquitoes irritate the reindeer. At the end, Valentina Axmetova tells how she once secretly collected enough reindeer hooves to make meat jelly, providing the herders with a pleasant surprise for breakfast the next day.
Citation: Valentina Axmetova. In the reindeer herd / Работа чумработницы. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Protective doll / Хранитель оленей
Description: In this little text Valentina Axmetova tells about the wife of one of her older brothers, who was a shaman. During a trip by reindeer to the village called Tva- jan, when the brother, his wife, and an old reindeer herder were by themselves, she took out an old leather doll that she had inherited from her mother. This doll watched over the reindeer so that they didn’t need to be watched by the humans.
Citation: Evdokija Adukanova. Protective doll / Хранитель оленей. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: To school / В школе
Description: In this excerpt Evdokija Adukanova tells of her first year in boarding school in Esso. She was nine years old at the time and missed her father terribly. Luckily her older brother looked after her very well. At the end of the school year she and other children were taken back home by some reindeer herders. When she got home to the little settlement Laučan (Figure 1) and saw her mother chopping ɲaːlakʨa (finely chopped fresh raw offal, a delicacy, see Figure 6.1), her emotions got the better of her and she burst into tears.
Citation: Evdokija Adukanova. To school / В школе. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Childhood memoirs / Воспоминания про детство
Description: The text begins with some of the earliest memories of Raisa Solodikova, when she lived with her parents in the reindeer herd: she remembers how her younger brother was born and how he nearly crawled into the fire when he was six months old. When she was about five, the family moved to the village Tvajan (Figure 1), where she saw many items for the first time, for example lump sugar, which she used to play knucklebones with. Dried fruit she mistook for mush- rooms, wondering why her father had bought those when so many grew in the forest. After finishing the Tvajan primary school the children had to go to boarding school in Esso, and at the end of the school year they were brought back home by people who worked in the collective farm. The journey on horseback and on foot could take up to 12 days in bad weather. It took them past Ichinsky (Figure 7.1), a volcano in the Sredinny Range in Central Kamchatka, and through several reindeer herds, where the herders welcomed the children with freshly slaughtered reindeer meat and raw offal. In summer Raisa Solodikova’s family moved to a fishing camp, and the children who still went to primary school would walk the three kilometres to school from there every day. She had to help her father by bringing fish he had caught to neighbours, and once got a fright when the moon shone out behind clouds, giving her the feeling it was chasing her.
Citation: Raisa Solodikova. Childhood memoirs / Воспоминания про детство. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Modes of transport / Транспорт до появления машин
Description: Rimma Egorova tells how she used to go sledding with her younger siblings and cousins while her parents were at work, sometimes even taking a dog sled. This leads her to describe how in winter dog sleds were the main means of transport of both goods and people; in summer this transport was done with horses. She mentions how her older siblings had to come back from boarding school by horseback and how the family used to wait for them, leaving for the fishing camp when they finally arrived. At the fishing camp her mother had to prepare a lot of dried fish for the collective farm. This way of life continued even after the inhabitants of Tvajan were resettled in Bystraja (Figure 1), an abandoned logging camp.
Citation: Rimma Egorova. Modes of transport / Транспорт до появления машин. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: At the fishing camp / На рыбалке
Description: This tells of a summer when Natalija Tylkanova was about six years old, when she stayed with her grandmother in a fishing camp. With them were another old couple, husband and wife (the Istap and Konna referred to in Text 10, line 9), and a half-blind old woman сalled Irina. The husband fished, and Natalija Tylkanova’s grandmother and the wife spent all day until late in the evening cleaning the fish and hanging it up to dry (Figure 9.1). The half-blind old Irina was with them because there was no-one in the village to look after her, since everybody was working in the fields of the collective farm or making hay. Natalija Tylkanova’s grandmother got very irritated with Irina because she would disappear some- where as soon as the women who had cleaned fish got back to camp. At the end Natalija Tylkanova told her grandmother that Irina was going to the smokehouse every evening (probably to check how much had been produced that day).
Citation: Natalija Tylkanova. At the fishing camp / На рыбалке. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Blue eyes / Голубоглазый
Description: This little anecdote was narrated after the previous one (Text 9) and hence con- tains references to people who were introduced before. Natalija Tylkanova tells how a fellow villager visited the fishing camp on the Icha river (Figure 10.1) where she was staying with her grandmother, in order to do some fishing for himself. He surprised the little girl with his blue eyes. The narrative evokes how isolated the fishing camps are and how much their inhabitants thirst for news about life in the village.
Citation: Natalija Tylkanova. Blue eyes / Голубоглазый. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.

Name: Hunting and fishing / Охотник
Description: Artёm Solodikov tells how he was a reindeer herder for six years, working with his parents, until he became a hunter in 1981 and moved to the Managič river (see Figure 3.1 in Section 3.1 for a photo of the homestead), where he was joined by his parents and younger brother. He lists the different animals he hunts (sable, foxes, ermine, wolverines, bears, capercaillies, ptarmigans, ducks) in winter, going to the district centre Esso around New Year and in February to deliver his furs. In summer he fishes for various salmonids, mostly with fish traps and nets, though occasionally also with a pole hook elge (Figure 11.1), and also works for the State Commercial Agency as a construction worker.
Citation: Artёm Solodikov. Hunting and fishing / Охотник. in Pakendorf, Brigitte (ed.), I always migrated by reindeer: Lamunkhin and Bystraja Even narratives about their traditional way of life. Berlin: Language Science Press.
